questionText: A regression test suite takes 3 hours to complete. The team wants it to run regularly without blocking developers during business hours. What is the recommended pipeline strategy?
options: Run the full suite on every commit, blocking the pipeline until complete
Schedule the regression suite as a nightly batch job so the team has a clear picture of SUT quality each morning without blocking daytime development
Split the suite into 1-minute micro-suites run every hour
Reduce the suite until it runs in under 10 minutes
explanation: For longer-running test suites, running them as a nightly regression (scheduled batch job) is the recommended practice. The team has a clear picture of SUT quality each morning without blocking the development pipeline during the day.

questionText: After a nightly run, test case TC_045 ("Process refund for cancelled order") fails. The TAF log shows step 3 failed: "Assert refund status = PROCESSED, actual = PENDING". The SUT API log shows the refund service returned HTTP 200 with status="PENDING". Screenshots confirm the UI also shows "PENDING". What is the correct conclusion and next action?
options: The TAS has a bug — the assertion logic is wrong
The SUT has a defect — the refund service is returning PENDING when it should return PROCESSED after a cancelled order; log a defect with the TAF log, SUT API log, and screenshots as evidence
The test environment is unavailable — all tests should be re-run
This is a flaky test — mark it as skipped and monitor
explanation: Following the 5-step analysis: step 3 failed (TAS logs this); the SUT state (API returned PENDING, UI shows PENDING) does NOT match the expected state (PROCESSED). Since the actual vs expected mismatch is in the SUT, not the TAS (assertion is correct, SUT returned the wrong value), a defect should be logged with all evidence.

questionText: TC_112 fails with error: "Element not found: #submit-button". The SUT application loads correctly in a manual browser test. A developer reviews the screenshot and confirms the submit button is visible on screen. What type of failure is this most likely, and what should the TAE investigate?
options: SUT defect — the submit button code has a bug
TAS failure — the element locator (#submit-button) in the page object is likely broken (the SUT may have changed the element ID or the selector is wrong); this is a TAS issue, not a SUT defect
Network connectivity issue — retry the test
Environment outage — check all other tests
explanation: When the actual and expected results of the SUT match (button is visually present and functional) but the TAS reports failure, the defect is most likely in the TAS — a broken locator in the page object. This is classified as a "TAS failure" (test execution status = TAS failure, not SUT defect). The TAE should update the locator in the page object.

questionText: The TAE needs to send the weekly test report. She has three audiences: (1) the CTO who wants to know release readiness, (2) the product owner who wants to know which user stories are verified, (3) the senior developer who wants to see which specific API calls are failing. What approach is correct?
options: Send the same detailed technical log to all three audiences

Send three tailored reports: (1) CTO gets trend summary, pass/fail ratio, overall quality gates; (2) PO gets coverage by user story/feature; (3) developer gets specific failing test steps, API logs, error messages — different detail levels for management, operational, and technical stakeholders
Only the test manager should receive the report
Publish one public dashboard that all stakeholders self-serve
explanation: Reports vary by audience: management stakeholders (CTO) focus on trends, pass-fail ratio, TAS reliability; operational stakeholders (PO) focus on product/feature coverage; technical stakeholders (developer) focus on lower-level details like failing steps and logs. Sending the same report to all wastes their time and buries relevant information.

questionText: A test case fails intermittently. The TAF log shows the failure occurred at 14:23:07. The TAE searches the SUT application log for entries at 14:23:07 but finds hundreds of unrelated log entries making correlation impossible. What logging improvement would solve this?
options: Add more sleep() statements to reduce log volume

Implement correlation IDs (trace IDs) — the TAS generates or captures a unique ID per test interaction and logs it; the SUT logs the same ID for each request, allowing the TAE to filter SUT logs by the exact correlation ID to trace the failure
Reduce test execution speed to spread out log entries
Switch to manual testing for intermittent failures
explanation: A correlation ID / trace ID is a unique ID added to each interaction. The TAS logs this ID with the test execution; the SUT logs the same ID for each request. This allows the TAE to filter the SUT log for exactly the entries corresponding to that test run, making root cause analysis of intermittent failures tractable.

questionText: A TAE is onboarding a new team member who has pushed test scripts to the shared repository. A static analysis scan of the test code reveals: a database password in plaintext in the test script, an API key hardcoded in a helper class, and a deprecated library with a known CVE. All test code is stored in the same repo as application code. Prioritise the actions.
options: Only fix the CVE as it affects the application; test code security is less important

Immediately rotate the exposed database password and API key (they are compromised by being in the repo); update the library to fix the CVE; enforce a policy that credentials must use environment variables or secrets management, never hardcoded — test code security is as important as application code security
Ask the new team member to re-read the clean code guidelines
Run the tests to verify they still work after removing the credentials
explanation: Even though test code is not deployed with software, credentials in test code are a real security risk — especially in shared repos. The syllabus explicitly states TAEs must extend security scanning to test automation code. Plaintext passwords and API keys must be treated as compromised immediately. Static analysis tools detect exactly these violations.

questionText: A TAE adds a new TAF feature: a custom wait mechanism that polls for element visibility instead of using hardcoded waits. The first test using this feature passes in CI. A week later, 5 tests using this feature start timing out inconsistently. What verification step was missed?
options: The tests should have used hardcoded waits instead

When a new TAF feature is first used, it should be verified and monitored closely; the initial single passing test was insufficient — the TAE should have run a representative sample of tests using the feature and monitored for edge cases before declaring it stable
The timeout is a SUT performance issue, not a TAF problem
The feature should be removed and manually implemented in each test
explanation: The syllabus states: "The first time a new feature of the TAF is used in test cases, it should be verified and monitored closely to ensure the feature is working correctly." One passing test is not sufficient verification — a broader set of tests and edge cases should be covered before considering the feature stable.

questionText: TC_200 passes locally on the TAE's machine but fails in the CI pipeline with "StaleElementReferenceException". The test clicks a button and immediately reads a value from a dynamically-loaded table. This works locally because the TAE's machine is faster. What is the root cause and correct fix?
options: The CI pipeline has insufficient resources — upgrade the build agent

The root cause is a hardcoded implicit wait or no wait mechanism — the test reads the table before it finishes loading in slower CI environments; fix by implementing dynamic polling (wait until the table element is present/stable) instead of relying on execution speed
The test has a bug in the assertion logic
Increase the test timeout globally in the CI configuration
explanation: StaleElementReferenceException when clicking then immediately reading a dynamic element is a classic hardcoded/no-wait anti-pattern. Locally it works because fast execution happens to outpace the DOM update; CI is slower so the element is stale. Fix: dynamic polling — wait until the element is present and stable before reading. This is the "dynamic waiting by polling" improvement from Ch8.

questionText: A TAF has 200 tests. Analysis of failure patterns shows: (A) 40 tests use Thread.sleep(3000) and fail when the SUT is slow, (B) 30 tests use a custom polling loop with no timeout and occasionally hang forever, (C) 20 tests subscribe to the SUT's "pageLoaded" event — these never fail. Rank these three approaches and recommend the correct fix for A and B.
options: All three approaches are equivalent; use whichever is easier to implement

(C) event subscription is best but requires SUT support; (A) hardcoded waits are the worst — they are a root cause of failures and must be replaced with dynamic polling; (B) polling is correct in concept but missing a timeout — add a timeout mechanism to prevent infinite hangs; migrate A to dynamic polling with timeout
(A) hardcoded waits are fine for slow environments, increase the sleep duration
Remove all wait mechanisms and rely on test retry logic
explanation: Three wait mechanisms ranked: hardcoded waits (worst — root cause of flakiness, unpredictable) → dynamic polling with timeout (correct — flexible, efficient, safe) → event subscription (best — most reliable, requires SUT to expose events). Polling without timeout is dangerous (infinite hang on SUT defect). Each category has a specific correct implementation.

questionText: A REST API returns a JSON response with 12 mandatory fields, each with specific types (string, integer, boolean). The TAE currently writes 12 individual assertions per test. A new service has 8 endpoints, each requiring similar type validation. Which approach would significantly reduce the assertion code while increasing coverage?
options: Write fewer assertions per test to reduce maintenance overhead

Implement schema validation — define a JSON schema specifying all mandatory fields and their types; the schema validation tool checks all 12 fields automatically for all 8 endpoints, replacing 96 individual assertions with schema definitions that are easier to maintain and more reliable
Use BDD to describe the expected response in natural language
Log the response and manually inspect it after each test run
explanation: Schema validation can replace large numbers of individual assertions. A JSON schema defines mandatory fields and their types; validation tools check the entire response against the schema automatically. For 8 endpoints × 12 fields = 96 potential assertions, schema validation dramatically reduces code while increasing coverage and making the validation easy to update when the API changes.

questionText: A TAE reviews the TAF and finds: 15 test cases all begin with the same 8-step user registration sequence hardcoded inline. The registration API endpoint exists but is never used by tests. Each of the 15 tests takes 90 seconds because the registration UI is slow. What improvement should the TAE recommend?
options: Reduce the test suite to 3 tests to improve speed

Refactor the 8-step registration into a setup method that calls the registration API directly (bypassing the UI); this reduces the precondition from 90 seconds of UI interaction to a sub-second API call, and a single API-based setup method replaces 15 copies of the 8-step sequence
Run the 15 tests in parallel to reduce wall-clock time
Switch to BDD so the registration steps become reusable Given steps
explanation: Two improvements combined: (1) consolidate duplicated setup into a setup method (clean code, single point of maintenance), (2) use the API endpoint for preconditions instead of UI — the syllabus explicitly mentions "web service calls can be used to fulfil preconditions for UI tests (e.g., user registration)". This is faster, more reliable, and reduces maintenance to one place.

questionText: A TAF initialises a new browser driver instance for every test method across 500 tests. Tests run in parallel and browser instances multiply until memory is exhausted. Which design pattern addresses this, and how?
options: Page Object Model — create a page class that manages driver lifecycle

Singleton Pattern — ensure only one driver instance is created and shared; for parallel execution, use a thread-local singleton pattern so each thread has exactly one driver instance rather than creating new instances per test method
Facade Pattern — hide the driver creation behind an interface
Flow Model Pattern — add a driver management layer on top of page objects
explanation: The Singleton Pattern is used to ensure only one driver communicates with the SUT. For parallel execution, a thread-local singleton gives each thread exactly one driver instance, preventing the driver explosion that causes memory exhaustion when new instances are created per test method.

questionText: A TAE is consulted during the design phase of a new IoT device firmware. She recommends adding three things: (1) a diagnostic interface that exposes internal sensor readings, (2) a command injection port for sending test commands without a physical UI, (3) architecture documentation mapping all interfaces. Which testability aspect does each recommendation address?
options: All three recommendations address controllability

(1) addresses observability — the interface gives insight into SUT state; (2) addresses controllability — the command port allows test cases to perform actions on the SUT; (3) addresses architecture transparency — documentation maps interfaces enabling testing at all levels
(1) and (2) address observability; (3) addresses controllability
All three are optional enhancements, not testability requirements
explanation: The three testability aspects: observability (SUT provides interfaces for insight into its state — the diagnostic interface), controllability (SUT provides interfaces for performing actions — the command injection port), and architecture transparency (documentation provides clear interfaces at all test levels). This is a direct application of section 2.1.1.

questionText: Two microservices teams are setting up contract testing. Team A (provider) wants to define how their service behaves and publish a specification. Team B (consumer) wants to define what they expect from the provider and have their expectations automatically verified. Which approaches do Team A and Team B respectively represent?
options: Team A = consumer-driven, Team B = provider-driven

Team A = provider-driven contract testing (provider creates the contract showing how its services operate); Team B = consumer-driven contract testing (consumer sets expectations determining how the provider should respond)
Both teams are using the same approach
Team A is doing integration testing, Team B is doing contract testing
explanation: Provider-driven contract testing: the provider creates the contract showing how its services operate (Team A). Consumer-driven contract testing: the consumer sets its expectation determining how the provider shall respond to requests (Team B). These are the two named approaches in the syllabus section 5.1.3.

questionText: A TAF team wants to manage different types of work in source control. Which branching strategy is recommended for test automation code?
options: Use a single "main" branch for all changes to keep things simple
Use different branches for features, releases, and defect fixes — this makes branch contents clear and supports understanding what each branch contains
Use one branch per test case
Use a branch per test environment
explanation: The clean code principles section recommends using an agreed branching structure and strategy in version control. Using different branches for features, releases, and defect fixes is helpful in understanding the branch contents — this mirrors standard software development branching practices.

questionText: Which of the following describes how AI/ML is applied to test automation log analysis?
options: AI replaces the need for a TAE entirely by writing and maintaining all test scripts

ML algorithms can automate analysis of large amounts of test log data to help TAEs find broken locators, analyse the reason for test failures (SUT defect vs TAS defect), and group common defects for reporting
AI tools can only be used for performance testing
ML is only applicable to UI test automation, not API tests
explanation: The syllabus states: ML algorithms help TAEs reduce time spent finding broken locators, analysing the reason for test failures (is it a SUT defect or TAS defect?), and grouping common defects for test reporting. AI/ML is a productivity tool for TAEs, not a replacement.

questionText: A CI/CD dashboard shows a test histogram of the last 30 days. TC_077 appears in the "failed" column 22 out of 30 days. TC_088 has never appeared in the "failed" column. TC_099 fails 3–4 days after each major release. What action does the test histogram suggest for each?
options: Ignore TC_077 as it is probably a known issue; run TC_088 more often; investigate TC_099 only if it fails 5 times

TC_077: identify and refactor — it is fragile and likely has a structural issue; TC_088: maintain as is — it is reliable; TC_099: investigate post-release regression pattern — there may be a dependency or data setup issue triggered by releases
Delete TC_077 as it provides no value; skip TC_099 on release days
Run TC_077 and TC_099 manually to verify they work
explanation: The test histogram enables TAEs to identify fragile test cases (TC_077, failing 73% of runs — refactor) and select those for improvement. Stable tests (TC_088) should be maintained. Patterns (TC_099 failing post-release) suggest regression analysis — the histogram reveals trends that drive targeted improvement decisions.

questionText: A team's automated UI tests show a page load time of 8 seconds, but real users report 2-second load times. Developers cannot reproduce the 8-second load in manual testing. What is the likely explanation?
options: The SUT has a performance defect that only affects automated tests

The TAS is tightly coupled to the SUT and its presence within the SUT environment may affect performance — this is the "intrusiveness" of automated test tools; the test environment with the TAS active differs from normal operation
The test environment has insufficient resources
The automated tests are measuring the wrong metric
explanation: The syllabus explicitly covers intrusiveness: "when the TAS is located within the SUT environment, the SUT's functionality may differ from when tests are conducted manually, potentially impacting performance." The TAS's presence can cause observable performance differences — a high level of intrusion can show failures not evident in production.

questionText: A team evaluates three automation tools. Tool X supports GUI and API testing, integrates with Jira and Jenkins, has a large open-source community, and uses Java. Tool Y supports GUI only, integrates with their test management system, and is vendor-supported with SLA. Tool Z supports API testing only, is free, and requires Python. The SUT is a Java web app with both UI and API layers. The team uses Java and Jenkins. What does a thorough comparison matrix analysis conclude?
options: Always choose the cheapest tool to minimise cost

Tool X best matches the critical requirements: both GUI and API coverage, Java language match (team proficiency + debugging efficiency), Jenkins CI/CD integration. Tool Y cannot cover API testing. Tool Z cannot cover GUI. A combination of X (primary) could be considered, but X alone meets all stated requirements
Tool Y because vendor SLA reduces risk
Tool Z because free tools have no licensing cost
explanation: The comparison matrix evaluates tools against requirements. Requirements here: GUI+API support, Java language, Jenkins integration. Tool X meets all. Tool Y fails the API requirement. Tool Z fails the GUI requirement and language match. The matrix conclusion: Tool X is the recommended choice. Language match provides cross-training and debugging benefits with the Java dev team.

questionText: A company has two products built on React and a third on Angular. The React TAEs have built a robust Core Libraries layer covering logging, reporting, test data utilities, and environment configuration — all technology-agnostic. Can the Angular TAF reuse this core layer?
options: No — core libraries are always SUT-specific and cannot be shared

Yes, if the Core Libraries layer contains only SUT-independent utilities (logging, reporting, test data utilities, environment config), it can be reused by the Angular project's TAF; each project then builds its own Business Logic layer on top of the shared core
Only if the Angular app is rewritten in React
Only the logging module can be shared, not the others
explanation: The Core Libraries layer stores libraries that are independent of any SUT — they can be reused across any project sharing the same development stack (or in this case, even across different stacks if the utilities are truly SUT-agnostic). Each project builds its own Business Logic layer on top. This is the scaling pattern described in section 3.1.3.

questionText: An SUT release adds a new "Express Checkout" feature behind a feature toggle. Not all test environments have this toggle enabled. Some test suites should only run the Express Checkout tests when the toggle is on. How should testware configuration management handle this?
options: Create completely separate test suites that are manually selected by the team before each run

Use feature toggle configuration in the testware — define the toggle state per test environment; test cases for Express Checkout are tagged and the feature toggle controls whether these test suites execute on a given environment, automatically excluding them where the feature is not enabled
Run all tests including Express Checkout on all environments and mark failures as expected
Duplicate the entire test suite into a "with toggle" and "without toggle" version
explanation: Feature toggle configuration is one of the two valid testware versioning approaches in the syllabus: "A feature toggle configuration can be defined per each release or test environment. The feature toggle can be used in the testware to identify which test suites to execute on a given release/test environment."

questionText: A QA team spends 2 hours before every sprint manually creating 50 test user accounts with different roles and permissions in each new test environment. The user registration API exists and is well-documented. How can test automation tools reduce this overhead?
options: Hire more QA staff to do the manual setup faster

Write an automation script that calls the user registration API to create all 50 user accounts with the correct roles — this is an "environment setup and control" use of test automation tools, completing in seconds what takes 2 hours manually, and can be run as a pipeline step when a new environment is provisioned
Ask developers to pre-populate the database directly
Use production user data in test environments
explanation: Environment setup and control is a non-testing use of test automation: "In a situation where users with multiple profiles need to be created based on different data inputs, a team can use an automated test script to call a web service endpoint that registers these users." This is exactly the scenario — the API-based setup script replaces 2 hours of manual work.

questionText: After a sprint, the TAE publishes a test report. The test manager emails back: "I need to know which test cases were added this sprint, whether the pass rate improved compared to last sprint, and whether any test suites are consistently failing." Which of these are analysis dimensions the test reporting system should support?
options: Only the current pass/fail count matters; historical comparisons are unnecessary

All three: tracking new test cases added per sprint, comparing pass rate trends across runs, and identifying test suites with frequent regressions — these are all standard test progress report analysis capabilities that help management stakeholders make release decisions
Only the last dimension (frequent failures) is a valid report metric
Test reports should only be generated for failed test runs
explanation: The syllabus covers all three: (1) test cases added since last run is a management trend metric; (2) pass-fail ratio changes are a key trend management focuses on; (3) keeping history to gather statistics on test suites with frequent regressions is explicitly recommended for trend analysis. All three together form the core of a management-level test progress report.
